questions.stem: At a FinTech payment processor building a real-time fraud detection lakehouse, the data engineering team must ingest streaming card transactions, compute 5-minute rolling velocity aggregates in real time, and land the enriched records as Apache Parquet files in Amazon S3 with the LEAST operational overhead. Select and order the 4 architectural steps from initial ingestion to S3 storage.
options: Order 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4: (1) Ingest raw card events into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams -> (2) Process stateful 5-minute sliding windows using Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink -> (3) Emit enriched aggregates to an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream configured with inline Parquet conversion via a Glue Data Catalog table schema -> (4) Deliver the compressed Parquet partitions directly into the target Amazon S3 bucket.
Order 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 3: (1) Process windows in Flink -> (2) Ingest into Kinesis Data Streams -> (3) Write raw CSV to S3 -> (4) Run Data Firehose on S3 files.
Order 1 -> 3 -> 2 -> 4: (1) Ingest into Kinesis Data Streams -> (2) Land raw JSON in S3 via Firehose -> (3) Run Apache Flink directly on S3 cold storage -> (4) Convert to Parquet via SQS.
Order 3 -> 1 -> 2 -> 4: (1) Buffer in Data Firehose -> (2) Send to Kinesis Data Streams -> (3) Aggregate in Flink -> (4) Store in DynamoDB.
questions.explanation: In a real-time AWS streaming pipeline, events first enter Amazon Kinesis Data Streams (Step 1), are aggregated over stateful windows by Managed Service for Apache Flink (Step 2), pass to Amazon Data Firehose with Glue Catalog schema conversion enabled for Apache Parquet (Step 3), and land partitioned in Amazon S3 (Step 4). Architectural Deep Dive: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams provides sub-second real-time stream ingestion with configurable retention (24 hours up to 365 days), replayability across multiple independent consumers, and optional Enhanced Fan-Out (2 MB/s dedicated throughput per consumer per shard via HTTP/2). Why Distractors Fail: Option B (Order 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 3: (1) Process windows in Flink -> (2) Ingest into Kin...) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and uses a non-replayable delivery buffer or competing queue where multiple independent consumers cannot replay historical stream records at their own pace. Option C (Order 1 -> 3 -> 2 -> 4: (1) Ingest into Kinesis Data Streams -> (2) Land ra...) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and uses a non-replayable delivery buffer or competing queue where multiple independent consumers cannot replay historical stream records at their own pace. Option D (Order 3 -> 1 -> 2 -> 4: (1) Buffer in Data Firehose -> (2) Send to Kinesis ...) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and uses a non-replayable delivery buffer or competing queue where multiple independent consumers cannot replay historical stream records at their own pace.
questions.use_case: High-velocity clickstream and payment fraud pipelines ingest events into Kinesis Data Streams in On-Demand mode (or Provisioned shards with 1 MB/s write and 2 MB/s read per shard) so Apache Flink, AWS Lambda, and Firehose can all read the exact same stream concurrently.
questions.hack: Multiple consumers needing real-time replay + ordering per PartitionKey = Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use Enhanced Fan-Out when multiple consumers need dedicated 2 MB/s read bandwidth without throttling.

questions.stem: An e-commerce marketplace ingesting millions of real-time clickstream and order events per hour has a data engineering squad that is currently captures website clickstream events. Three applications must each process every event within seconds, reading at their own pace. A fraud-model team plans to add a fourth application next month, and it must be able to start from the events captured earlier that same day. Which ingestion service should the data platform engineer use?
options: An Amazon Data Firehose stream that delivers to Amazon S3.
An Amazon SNS topic with an SQS queue for each application.
An Amazon SQS standard queue shared by the applications.
An Amazon Kinesis data stream in on-demand capacity mode.
questions.explanation: - **a** Firehose buffers and delivers records to a destination; it has no consumer API, so applications cannot each read the events within seconds, and the S3 copy arrives only after the buffer interval. - **b** SNS-to-SQS fan-out serves the three current applications, but SNS standard topics keep no history: a queue subscribed next month only receives events published after it subscribes. - **c** Consumers of one SQS queue compete for messages: each message goes to one consumer and is deleted after processing, so the applications would not each see every event. - **d** A Kinesis data stream retains records (24 hours by default) whether or not they were read, lets several consumers read the same records independently, and lets a new consumer start from TRIM_HORIZON or a timestamp to pick up earlier events. **The concept.** Kinesis Data Streams is a retained, multi-consumer stream; Firehose is delivery only, SQS is a competing-consumer queue, and SNS standard topics deliver only to current subscribers. **Why this is correct.** Two requirements decide it: every application reads every event independently, and a consumer added later must read events from earlier in the day. A Kinesis data stream keeps records for its retention period regardless of consumption, so any number of consumers read the same data at their own positions and a new one can start from the oldest retained record. SNS plus SQS meets the first requirement but not the second, a shared SQS queue meets neither, and Firehose exposes no read API at all. **How to reason it out** 1. Note the latency (seconds) and that every application needs every event. 2. Note the late-joining consumer: it needs events that were published before it existed. 3. Eliminate designs without retention a new reader can rewind into (SNS, SQS, Firehose). 4. Choose the retained multi-consumer stream: Kinesis Data Streams. > **Exam tip:** Many independent readers plus a late joiner that needs past events means a retained stream, not a queue, topic or delivery stream. Architectural Deep Dive: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams provides sub-second real-time stream ingestion with configurable retention (24 hours up to 365 days), replayability across multiple independent consumers, and optional Enhanced Fan-Out (2 MB/s dedicated throughput per consumer per shard via HTTP/2). Why Distractors Fail: Option A (An Amazon Data Firehose stream that delivers to Amazon S3....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and requires managing custom stream consumer infrastructure when the requirement is zero-administration delivery into S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch. Option B (An Amazon SNS topic with an SQS queue for each application....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and sets a short Visibility Timeout while the consumer takes several minutes to process messages (causing duplicate processing by other consumers) or uses Short Polling (WaitTimeSeconds=0) that burns money on empty API responses. Option C (An Amazon SQS standard queue shared by the applications....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and sets a short Visibility Timeout while the consumer takes several minutes to process messages (causing duplicate processing by other consumers) or uses Short Polling (WaitTimeSeconds=0) that burns money on empty API responses.
questions.use_case: High-velocity clickstream and payment fraud pipelines ingest events into Kinesis Data Streams in On-Demand mode (or Provisioned shards with 1 MB/s write and 2 MB/s read per shard) so Apache Flink, AWS Lambda, and Firehose can all read the exact same stream concurrently.
questions.hack: Multiple consumers needing real-time replay + ordering per PartitionKey = Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use Enhanced Fan-Out when multiple consumers need dedicated 2 MB/s read bandwidth without throttling.

questions.stem: At a connected-vehicle telemetry company streaming sensor payloads into AWS, the lead data architect is currently ingests article-view events into an Amazon Kinesis data stream. Traffic changes unpredictably from hour to hour, and the operations team does not want to forecast, monitor or adjust shard counts. Which configuration meets these requirements while minimizing ongoing operational maintenance?
options: Switch the data stream to on-demand capacity mode.
Replace the data stream with an Amazon MSK provisioned cluster.
Keep provisioned mode with enough shards for the busiest hour.
Keep provisioned mode and call UpdateShardCount from an alarm.
questions.explanation: - **a** On-demand mode manages shards for you and scales write and read capacity with observed traffic, so there is no shard count to forecast or adjust. - **b** An MSK provisioned cluster moves the capacity problem to brokers and partitions, adding operational work rather than removing it. - **c** Sizing for the peak still requires forecasting the peak and paying for idle shards the rest of the time, and an unforecast spike still throttles. - **d** Alarm-driven resharding works, but the team then owns the alarm thresholds, the scaling function and the UpdateShardCount quotas, which is exactly the capacity management they want to avoid. **The concept.** Kinesis Data Streams has two capacity modes: provisioned (you choose and change the shard count) and on-demand (AWS scales shards with traffic). **Why this is correct.** The deciding constraint is that nobody wants to plan or change capacity. On-demand mode removes shard management entirely. Alarm-driven UpdateShardCount and peak sizing both keep provisioned mode, so someone still forecasts or automates capacity, and MSK provisioned adds broker management. **How to reason it out** 1. Identify the workload: unpredictable traffic with no capacity planning wanted. 2. Compare provisioned options: both still require choosing or automating a shard count. 3. Pick the mode in which AWS manages shards: on-demand. > **Exam tip:** Unpredictable traffic and no shard management means Kinesis on-demand capacity mode. Architectural Deep Dive: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams provides sub-second real-time stream ingestion with configurable retention (24 hours up to 365 days), replayability across multiple independent consumers, and optional Enhanced Fan-Out (2 MB/s dedicated throughput per consumer per shard via HTTP/2). Why Distractors Fail: Option B (Replace the data stream with an Amazon MSK provisioned cluster....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and uses a non-replayable delivery buffer or competing queue where multiple independent consumers cannot replay historical stream records at their own pace. Option C (Keep provisioned mode with enough shards for the busiest hour....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and uses a non-replayable delivery buffer or competing queue where multiple independent consumers cannot replay historical stream records at their own pace. Option D (Keep provisioned mode and call UpdateShardCount from an alarm....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and uses a non-replayable delivery buffer or competing queue where multiple independent consumers cannot replay historical stream records at their own pace.
questions.use_case: High-velocity clickstream and payment fraud pipelines ingest events into Kinesis Data Streams in On-Demand mode (or Provisioned shards with 1 MB/s write and 2 MB/s read per shard) so Apache Flink, AWS Lambda, and Firehose can all read the exact same stream concurrently.
questions.hack: Multiple consumers needing real-time replay + ordering per PartitionKey = Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use Enhanced Fan-Out when multiple consumers need dedicated 2 MB/s read bandwidth without throttling.

questions.stem: [A capital markets risk-reporting organization running regulated analytics pipelines on AWS has a data engineer who] An on-premises Oracle database supports a live ordering system. A data engineer must copy the existing order rows into an Amazon S3 data lake and then keep S3 current with every insert, update and delete, while placing minimal load on the source. Which approach should the engineer use?
options: An AWS DMS task of type full load and ongoing replication.
An AWS DMS task of type CDC, started from the current time.
A nightly AWS Glue JDBC job with bookmarks on the order ID.
An AWS DMS task of type full load, rerun each night.
questions.explanation: - **a** Full load plus CDC copies the existing rows once and then reads the database transaction log to apply inserts, updates and deletes continuously, with little load on the source. - **b** A CDC task without a full load captures changes from its start point but never copies the rows that already exist, so the lake would be missing historical orders. - **c** A bookmark on a monotonically increasing key picks up new rows, but it never sees updates or deletes to existing rows, and nightly runs are not continuous. - **d** A nightly full load re-reads every table each time, which loads the source heavily and leaves S3 up to a day behind. **The concept.** AWS DMS tasks come in three types: full load (one-time copy), CDC only (changes from a start point) and full load plus CDC (copy, then continuous changes read from the transaction log). **Why this is correct.** The requirement has two halves: the existing rows and every later change, including deletes. Full load and ongoing replication covers both and reads changes from the redo log rather than by querying tables. Full load alone misses continuity and hammers the source, CDC only misses history, and a Glue JDBC bookmark sees only newly inserted keys. **How to reason it out** 1. Split the requirement: historical rows plus continuous inserts, updates and deletes. 2. Note that deletes and updates require log-based change capture, not key-based incremental reads. 3. Match both halves to one DMS task type: full load plus CDC. > **Exam tip:** Existing data plus every later change from a relational source means an AWS DMS full-load-and-CDC task. Architectural Deep Dive: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) performs homogeneous and heterogeneous database migrations with minimal downtime using Full Load + Change Data Capture (CDC), while the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) converts heterogeneous database schemas, stored procedures, and views (for example, Oracle/SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL or Redshift). Why Distractors Fail: Option B (An AWS DMS task of type CDC, started from the current time....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and takes hours of production database downtime for a cold dump-and-restore or attempts heterogeneous schema conversion without AWS SCT. Option C (A nightly AWS Glue JDBC job with bookmarks on the order ID....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and re-scans the entire historical S3 bucket or table on every scheduled run, wasting DPU capacity and duplicating target records. Option D (An AWS DMS task of type full load, rerun each night....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and takes hours of production database downtime for a cold dump-and-restore or attempts heterogeneous schema conversion without AWS SCT.
questions.use_case: When migrating a 20 TB on-premises Oracle data warehouse to Amazon Redshift, engineers use AWS SCT Extraction Agents alongside DMS Full Load + CDC replication tasks.
questions.hack: Minimal downtime live database migration / continuous CDC replication = AWS DMS. Heterogeneous engine schema & PL/SQL conversion = AWS SCT + DMS.

questions.stem: [a multi-national logistics and supply-chain carrier tracking real-time shipment telemetry] Analysts use Amazon Athena to run monthly aggregate reports over the full history of a CSV data lake in Amazon S3. Each query reads 4 of the table's 120 columns across every row, and the Athena bill keeps rising. Which change reduces the data scanned per query by the LARGEST amount?
options: Partition the CSV data in S3 by the year and month of each event.
Move the CSV objects to the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access class.
Compress the CSV files with gzip and keep the same table layout.
Rewrite the data as Snappy-compressed Parquet with a Glue job.
questions.explanation: - **a** Partitioning prunes data only when queries filter on the partition columns. These reports aggregate the full history, so every partition is still read in full. - **b** A storage class changes the storage price, not the bytes Athena scans. Queries would scan the same data and also add retrieval charges. - **c** Athena bills on compressed bytes, so gzip does cut the scan, but every query still reads all 120 columns of every row. Columnar storage saves far more when queries touch 4 columns. - **d** Parquet is columnar, so Athena reads only the 4 referenced columns, and per-column compression shrinks those further. That attacks both the unused 116 columns and the raw size. **The concept.** Athena bills by bytes scanned. Row formats such as CSV force a query to read every column of every row; columnar formats such as Apache Parquet store each column separately so engines read only the referenced columns, and compress each column well. **Why this is correct.** Queries touching 4 of 120 columns waste roughly 97% of every CSV scan. Parquet removes that waste and adds compression on top, so it beats gzip CSV, which shrinks bytes but still reads every column. Partitioning is a strong lever only when queries filter on the partition key, and these full-history reports do not. Storage classes do not change scan volume at all. **How to reason it out** 1. Identify what Athena charges for: bytes scanned per query. 2. Note the access pattern: few columns, all rows, no selective filter. 3. Columnar layout removes unused columns from the scan; compression only shrinks what is still read. 4. Partitioning helps only with filters on the partition key, which these reports lack. > **Exam tip:** When queries read a few columns, columnar Parquet is the biggest scan-cost lever; partitioning helps only when queries filter on the partition key. Architectural Deep Dive: Amazon Athena is a serverless interactive query engine over S3 (charged at $5 per TB scanned): converting data to columnar Apache Parquet/ORC with Snappy compression, partitioning by high-frequency filter keys, and enabling Partition Projection (for highly predictable date/ID ranges without Glue Catalog metadata calls) cuts query latency and scan cost by up to 90-99%. Why Distractors Fail: Option A (Partition the CSV data in S3 by the year and month of each event....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and routes multi-gigabyte file uploads through a Lambda function or EC2 web tier instead of generating an S3 Pre-Signed URL for direct client-to-S3 upload, or forgets that S3 Pre-Signed URLs inherit the exact IAM permissions and session expiration of the principal that generated them. Option B (Move the CSV objects to the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access class....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and routes multi-gigabyte file uploads through a Lambda function or EC2 web tier instead of generating an S3 Pre-Signed URL for direct client-to-S3 upload, or forgets that S3 Pre-Signed URLs inherit the exact IAM permissions and session expiration of the principal that generated them. Option C (Compress the CSV files with gzip and keep the same table layout....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and writes hundreds of lines of raw CloudFormation boilerplate or attempts to run CodeDeploy EC2 shell scripts (`BeforeInstall`/`AfterInstall`) for serverless Lambda traffic shifting.
questions.use_case: To enforce FinOps cost guardrails across analyst teams, data engineers isolate teams into separate Athena Workgroups with 'Per-query data usage control' and 'Per-workgroup data usage alarms' in CloudWatch.
questions.hack: Slash Athena cost & speed up queries = Parquet/ORC + Partitioning + Partition Projection (avoids MSCK REPAIR TABLE / Glue Crawler metadata bottleneck). Control analyst spend = Athena Workgroup data scan limits.

questions.stem: [A digital media streaming platform analyzing viewer engagement across 40 countries has a data engineering team that] A data engineering team runs a nightly ETL pipeline made up of an AWS Glue crawler that catalogs new raw files, followed by two Glue Spark jobs that must run in sequence, each starting only after its predecessor succeeds. The team wants a single visual run graph with per-step status and does not want to provision or pay for an orchestration service beyond the ETL service they already use. What should the team use?
options: An AWS Glue workflow with a schedule trigger and conditional triggers.
An AWS Step Functions state machine with three .sync Glue task states.
An Amazon MWAA environment running a DAG with three Glue operators.
Amazon EventBridge rules matching each Glue job's state-change events.
questions.explanation: - **a** A Glue workflow chains the crawler and both jobs with a scheduled start trigger and conditional triggers that fire on the predecessor's success, and shows each run as a graph with per-node status, all inside AWS Glue at no extra orchestration cost. - **b** Step Functions would sequence the steps correctly, but it is an additional orchestration service billed per state transition, which the team does not want to add. - **c** MWAA can run Glue operators, but it is a separate always-on Airflow environment the team would have to provision and pay for, which the stem rules out. - **d** Rules on Glue state-change events can start the next step, but the chain is spread across separate rules with no single run graph or per-run view of the pipeline. **The concept.** AWS Glue workflows are the native orchestration feature for pipelines made only of Glue crawlers and jobs: triggers (scheduled, on-demand, conditional, event) form a dependency graph that is run and monitored inside AWS Glue. **Why this is correct.** Every step is a Glue entity and the team wants no orchestration service beyond Glue itself, plus one run graph. A Glue workflow provides exactly that: a scheduled start trigger, conditional triggers that fire when the predecessor succeeds, and a per-run graph with node status. Step Functions and MWAA would both work functionally but add a separately billed service; EventBridge rules can chain jobs but give no single run view. **How to reason it out** 1. Check whether every step is a Glue crawler or Glue job; if so, Glue workflows can orchestrate it natively. 2. Apply the constraint: no extra orchestration service rules out Step Functions and MWAA even though both could run the jobs. 3. Check the monitoring need: one run graph with per-step status rules out a chain of separate EventBridge rules. 4. Build the workflow: scheduled start trigger on the crawler, conditional triggers on success for each job. > **Exam tip:** All-Glue pipeline plus no extra orchestration service means AWS Glue workflows; a non-Glue step is what pushes you to Step Functions. Architectural Deep Dive: AWS Glue Crawlers automatically inspect S3, Redshift, RDS, and DynamoDB data stores to infer schemas and populate the AWS Glue Data Catalog; configuring the crawler to 'Crawl new sub-folders only' or triggering it via S3 Event Notifications dramatically reduces crawl runtime and cost. Why Distractors Fail: Option B (An AWS Step Functions state machine with three .sync Glue task states....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and provisions unmanaged EC2 cron servers that lack dependency retries, dead-letter handling, and visual execution state tracking. Option C (An Amazon MWAA environment running a DAG with three Glue operators....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and provisions unmanaged EC2 cron servers that lack dependency retries, dead-letter handling, and visual execution state tracking. Option D (Amazon EventBridge rules matching each Glue job's state-change events....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and provisions unmanaged EC2 cron servers that lack dependency retries, dead-letter handling, and visual execution state tracking.
questions.use_case: Data lake teams configure Glue Crawlers with a RecrawlPolicy of CRAWL_NEW_FOLDERS_ONLY (or CRAWL_EVENT_MODE via SQS/S3 events) to register new daily partitions in seconds.
questions.hack: Speed up slow Glue Crawlers on massive S3 buckets = Crawl new sub-folders only OR use S3 Event Notifications + SQS event-driven crawlers.

questions.stem: [an InsurTech claims-processing firm consolidating relational and semi-structured data into Amazon S3 and Redshift] An AWS Glue Spark job reads a 3 TB clickstream table from Amazon S3 that is cataloged with year, month and day partition columns. Each run needs only the last 7 days, but the script creates a DynamicFrame from the whole table and filters on the date afterwards. Runtime and DPU cost grow every week as history accumulates. Which change reduces runtime the most?
options: Apply the date filter as a Python UDF over the date columns once the table loads.
Pass a push_down_predicate on the partition columns in the DynamicFrame read.
Cache the DynamicFrame as a Spark DataFrame in memory before the date filter runs.
Add workers so each partition of the table is read in parallel before the filter.
questions.explanation: - **a** A Python UDF is opaque to the optimizer and adds JVM-to-Python serialization, and it still runs after the full read, so nothing is pruned. - **b** A pushdown predicate is evaluated against the partition metadata in the Data Catalog before any file is read, so only the 7 matching day partitions are listed and loaded. - **c** Caching happens after the read; it speeds up repeated access to data that never needed to be loaded, and caching 3 TB adds memory pressure. - **d** More workers parallelize the waste: the job still lists and reads 3 TB to keep a few days of it, so DPU cost rises even if wall-clock time drops. **The concept.** Partition pruning: when a filter is expressed on partition columns at read time, the engine resolves which partitions match from catalog metadata and never opens the others. **Why this is correct.** The table is already partitioned by year/month/day, so the cheapest data is the data never read. Supplying push_down_predicate when creating the DynamicFrame (or filtering on partition columns before any action with the DataFrame API) prunes the read to 7 partitions. Adding workers, caching or using a UDF all act after the full 3 TB has been read; the UDF is worse still because it hides the predicate from the optimizer. **How to reason it out** 1. Notice that the filter column is the partition key and that only a small slice of partitions is needed. 2. Ask whether each option changes how much data is read or only how fast the full read runs. 3. Choose the option that applies the filter on partition columns at read time. 4. Reject options that act after the full read (workers, cache, UDF). > **Exam tip:** Filter on partition columns when you read (pushdown predicate), not after; reading less beats reading faster. Architectural Deep Dive: AWS Glue DynamicFrames handle messy, schema-evolving semi-structured data natively without requiring a rigid upfront pass: ResolveChoice resolves ambiguous column types, Relationalize flattens nested JSON structures, push_down_predicate filters S3 partitions before reading files into memory, and groupFiles='inPartition' coalesces thousands of small files. Why Distractors Fail: Option A (Apply the date filter as a Python UDF over the date columns once the table ...) fails to satisfy the specific performance, security, or managed-service constraint stated in the prompt. Option C (Cache the DynamicFrame as a Spark DataFrame in memory before the date filte...) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and loads unpartitioned raw Spark DataFrames into memory first, causing OutOfMemory (OOM) exceptions or schema inference failures. Option D (Add workers so each partition of the table is read in parallel before the f...) fails to satisfy the specific performance, security, or managed-service constraint stated in the prompt.
questions.use_case: When ingesting millions of 10 KB IoT JSON files from S3, Glue engineers combine push_down_predicate on partition columns with groupFiles='inPartition' and groupSize to prevent Spark driver OOM errors.
questions.hack: Glue Spark OOM / small-file problem = groupFiles='inPartition' + groupSize; filter partitions before S3 read = push_down_predicate; nested JSON flattening = Relationalize.

questions.stem: A genomics research institute processing high-volume sequencing metadata on AWS has a data platform engineer who maintains a mission-critical application that stores customer profiles in an Amazon DynamoDB table. A data engineer must run processing logic within seconds of any profile being created or modified, using the old and new versions of the item, without changing the application code. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Schedule incremental exports of the table to S3 and process each export.
Turn on DynamoDB Streams and add a Lambda event source mapping.
Run an AWS Glue job at five-minute intervals that scans the table.
Turn on DynamoDB Streams and read the stream with an AWS Glue streaming job.
questions.explanation: - **a** Incremental export to S3 works on export windows of at least 15 minutes, so changes are processed far later than within seconds. - **b** DynamoDB Streams records every item-level change, with the NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES view type supplying both versions, and a Lambda event source mapping invokes the function within seconds without any change to the writer. - **c** A scheduled scan consumes read capacity, cannot see the previous version of an item, and runs minutes rather than seconds after the change. - **d** AWS Glue streaming jobs read from Kinesis Data Streams and Apache Kafka sources, not directly from a DynamoDB stream. **The concept.** DynamoDB Streams emits an ordered, item-level change record for every write; with the NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES view type each record carries the item before and after the change. **Why this is correct.** The table itself must be the trigger, because the application cannot change. DynamoDB Streams with a Lambda event source mapping reacts within seconds and provides old and new images. A Glue streaming job cannot use a DynamoDB stream as its source, and scheduled scans or incremental exports run minutes behind. **How to reason it out** 1. Note the constraints: seconds of latency, old and new item versions, no application changes. 2. Change data must come from the table itself: DynamoDB Streams with NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES. 3. Choose a consumer that reads DynamoDB Streams natively: a Lambda event source mapping. > **Exam tip:** React to DynamoDB item changes without touching the writer: DynamoDB Streams plus a Lambda event source mapping. Architectural Deep Dive: AWS Lambda executes serverless functions up to 15 minutes with 128 MB to 10 GB memory, 512 MB to 10 GB /tmp ephemeral storage, Lambda Layers for shared libraries/dependencies across functions, Provisioned Concurrency (or Lambda SnapStart for Java/Python/.NET) to eliminate cold starts, and Reserved Concurrency to guarantee and cap maximum concurrent executions for a specific function. Why Distractors Fail: Option A (Schedule incremental exports of the table to S3 and process each export....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and routes multi-gigabyte file uploads through a Lambda function or EC2 web tier instead of generating an S3 Pre-Signed URL for direct client-to-S3 upload, or forgets that S3 Pre-Signed URLs inherit the exact IAM permissions and session expiration of the principal that generated them. Option C (Run an AWS Glue job at five-minute intervals that scans the table....) fails to satisfy the specific performance, security, or managed-service constraint stated in the prompt. Option D (Turn on DynamoDB Streams and read the stream with an AWS Glue streaming job...) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and attempts to run strongly consistent reads against a Global Secondary Index (GSI) or tries to add a Local Secondary Index (LSI) to an existing table after creation.
questions.use_case: Latency-sensitive checkout APIs configure an Application Auto Scaling schedule on Lambda Provisioned Concurrency (pointed at a published function Version or Alias, never $LATEST) ahead of flash sales.
questions.hack: Eliminate Lambda cold starts = Provisioned Concurrency (or SnapStart for Java) on a Version/Alias. Cap a function so it doesn't overwhelm a downstream RDS DB = Reserved Concurrency. Share common SDKs/certs across functions = Lambda Layers.

questions.stem: At a SaaS customer-data platform (CDP) serving enterprise B2B tenants, the data pipeline team is currently stores user session data that is always read and written by session ID. Traffic peaks at millions of requests per second during sales events and is near zero overnight. Every acknowledged write must survive an infrastructure failure, latency must stay in single-digit milliseconds at any scale, and the team does not want to manage servers or capacity. Which data store meets these requirements?
options: Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 for MySQL.
Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey.
Amazon DynamoDB table in on-demand mode.
Amazon RDS for MySQL with read replicas.
questions.explanation: - **a** Aurora Serverless v2 removes instance sizing and is durable, but all writes still go through a single writer instance, so millions of writes per second with consistent single-digit-millisecond latency is not something a relational writer delivers. - **b** ElastiCache gives sub-millisecond reads and scales without node management, but it is a cache: replication to replicas is asynchronous, so a write acknowledged just before a failure can be lost. It does not meet the "every acknowledged write must survive" requirement as a system of record. - **c** Correct. DynamoDB is built for known-key reads and writes at any scale with consistent single-digit-millisecond latency and durably stores every write across multiple Availability Zones. On-demand mode scales with traffic without capacity units to plan; for an announced sales event that will far exceed previous peaks, the table can be pre-warmed with warm throughput. - **d** Read replicas scale reads only; writes still hit one primary instance whose size you manage. It fails both the write-throughput requirement and the "no capacity to manage" constraint. **The concept.** The access pattern picks the store. Known-key reads and writes at very high request rates with predictable latency are the DynamoDB use case; durability and serverless operations narrow it further. **Why this is correct.** Three constraints decide. Known-key access at millions of requests per second with consistent single-digit-millisecond latency rules out relational engines, which funnel writes through one writer. "Every acknowledged write must survive" rules out a cache, because ElastiCache replicates asynchronously. "No servers or capacity to manage" with traffic that swings from near zero to peak is what DynamoDB on-demand mode is for. On-demand instantly absorbs up to double a table's previous peak, so for a planned jump far beyond earlier traffic you set warm throughput in advance rather than managing capacity units. Aurora Serverless v2 is the tempting answer because it is serverless and durable, but it is still a single-writer relational database. **How to reason it out** 1. Identify the access pattern: every read and write is by session ID, a pure key/value pattern. 2. Apply the scale and latency requirement: millions of writes per second at single-digit milliseconds excludes single-writer relational engines. 3. Apply the durability requirement: a cache with asynchronous replication can lose acknowledged writes. 4. Apply the operations constraint: on-demand capacity removes capacity planning for spiky traffic. > **Exam tip:** Key/value access at any scale with durable writes and no capacity planning means DynamoDB on-demand; a cache is not a system of record and a relational writer does not scale out writes. Architectural Deep Dive: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams provides sub-second real-time stream ingestion with configurable retention (24 hours up to 365 days), replayability across multiple independent consumers, and optional Enhanced Fan-Out (2 MB/s dedicated throughput per consumer per shard via HTTP/2). Why Distractors Fail: Option A (Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 for MySQL....) fails to satisfy the specific performance, security, or managed-service constraint stated in the prompt. Option B (Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey....) fails to satisfy the specific performance, security, or managed-service constraint stated in the prompt. Option D (Amazon RDS for MySQL with read replicas....) fails to satisfy the specific performance, security, or managed-service constraint stated in the prompt.
questions.use_case: High-velocity clickstream and payment fraud pipelines ingest events into Kinesis Data Streams in On-Demand mode (or Provisioned shards with 1 MB/s write and 2 MB/s read per shard) so Apache Flink, AWS Lambda, and Firehose can all read the exact same stream concurrently.
questions.hack: Multiple consumers needing real-time replay + ordering per PartitionKey = Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use Enhanced Fan-Out when multiple consumers need dedicated 2 MB/s read bandwidth without throttling.

questions.stem: A smart-grid energy utility ingesting millions of smart-meter readings every minute has a data engineering team that is currently wants to power BI dashboards for 300 analysts who query throughout the business day. The queries join and aggregate several terabytes of historical sales data, scan most of each table, and group by region, product and week. The enterprise wants consistently fast response under this steady, all-day concurrent load. Which data store is the best fit?
options: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with read replicas.
An Amazon Redshift provisioned RA3 cluster.
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL on a larger instance.
Amazon Athena over partitioned Parquet in S3.
questions.explanation: - **a** Read replicas spread concurrent readers, but Aurora is a row-oriented OLTP engine. Full-table scans and aggregations over terabytes read every column of every row and run slowly on any replica. - **b** Correct. Redshift is a columnar, massively parallel warehouse: it reads only the referenced columns, compresses them, and spreads scans and aggregations across all slices, which is what steady, concurrent BI over terabytes needs. - **c** A bigger instance adds CPU and memory, but the row store still reads entire rows for column aggregates and runs each query on one node; it does not parallelize terabyte scans the way an MPP warehouse does. - **d** Athena suits ad hoc or infrequent queries and bills per terabyte scanned. For hundreds of analysts scanning most of several terabytes all day, per-query scan charges add up and response times are less consistent than a warehouse sized for the steady load. **The concept.** Analytical workloads (large scans, joins, group-by aggregations, BI concurrency) belong in a columnar MPP warehouse; row-oriented OLTP engines and per-query lake engines fit other access patterns. **Why this is correct.** The deciding signals are scan-heavy aggregation over terabytes and constant concurrent use. Redshift stores data by column and parallelizes each query across nodes, so it reads far less data and keeps latency steady. Athena is the cost answer when queries are occasional; with 300 analysts all day, scan-based pricing and variable latency make it the weaker choice. Aurora and RDS are row stores tuned for small transactional reads and writes; replicas or bigger instances do not change how they scan. **How to reason it out** 1. Classify the workload: large scans, joins and group-by aggregations are analytical (OLAP). 2. Note the usage profile: hundreds of concurrent users, steady all day. 3. Eliminate row-oriented OLTP engines, however they are scaled. 4. Choose between warehouse and lake query engine by frequency: steady heavy use favors Redshift; occasional use would favor Athena. > **Exam tip:** Scan-and-aggregate BI under steady concurrent load is Redshift; Athena wins only when queries are occasional. Architectural Deep Dive: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams provides sub-second real-time stream ingestion with configurable retention (24 hours up to 365 days), replayability across multiple independent consumers, and optional Enhanced Fan-Out (2 MB/s dedicated throughput per consumer per shard via HTTP/2). Why Distractors Fail: Option A (Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with read replicas....) fails to satisfy the specific performance, security, or managed-service constraint stated in the prompt. Option C (Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL on a larger instance....) fails to satisfy the specific performance, security, or managed-service constraint stated in the prompt. Option D (Amazon Athena over partitioned Parquet in S3....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and scans uncompressed CSV/JSON files across the entire S3 bucket or fails to enforce Athena Workgroup per-query data scan limits.

questions.hack: Multiple consumers needing real-time replay + ordering per PartitionKey = Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use Enhanced Fan-Out when multiple consumers need dedicated 2 MB/s read bandwidth without throttling.

questions.stem: [a global hospitality and travel booking network centralizing reservation analytics on AWS] A company keeps its datasets in Amazon S3 and queries them from Amazon Athena, Spark jobs on Amazon EMR, and Amazon Redshift Spectrum. Each engine holds its own table definitions, and they have drifted apart. The data team wants one shared set of schemas, locations, and partitions for all three engines, with no metadata servers to operate. What should the team use?
options: AWS Glue Data Catalog as the metastore for all three engines.
AWS Glue Schema Registry, with one registered schema per dataset.
An Apache Hive metastore on Amazon RDS shared by all three engines.
Amazon SageMaker Catalog, with each dataset published as an asset.
questions.explanation: - **a** The Glue Data Catalog is a serverless, Hive-compatible metastore. Athena uses it by default, EMR can be configured to use it as its metastore, and Redshift Spectrum external schemas point at its databases, so one definition serves all three. - **b** Schema Registry versions Avro, JSON Schema and Protobuf schemas for streaming producers and consumers. It records no table locations or partitions, and query engines do not resolve tables against it. - **c** A shared external Hive metastore can serve EMR, and Athena and Spectrum can be connected to one, but the team would then run and maintain the metastore service and its database, which the stem rules out. - **d** SageMaker Catalog is a business catalog: it adds descriptions, glossary terms and subscription workflows on top of technical assets. Engines still read schemas and partitions from a technical metastore, not from published assets. **The concept.** A technical data catalog stores table metadata (schema, format, location, partitions) once so every engine can query data where it lives. On AWS the managed technical catalog is the AWS Glue Data Catalog. **Why this is correct.** The requirement is one shared metadata source for three engines with no servers to run. The Glue Data Catalog meets both parts: Athena, EMR (as its Hive metastore) and Redshift Spectrum (through an external schema) all read the same tables. A Hive metastore on RDS would also give one shared definition, but it is infrastructure the team must operate. Schema Registry and SageMaker Catalog hold metadata of a different kind and are not metastores that query engines resolve tables against. **How to reason it out** 1. Identify the need: shared table definitions (schema, location, partitions) for several query engines. 2. Separate technical metastores from schema registries and business catalogs. 3. Of the two metastores, apply the constraint: no metadata servers to operate. 4. Choose the serverless Glue Data Catalog and point each engine at it. > **Exam tip:** Shared schemas, locations and partitions for Athena, EMR and Spectrum with nothing to run = the Glue Data Catalog. Architectural Deep Dive: AWS Glue Crawlers automatically inspect S3, Redshift, RDS, and DynamoDB data stores to infer schemas and populate the AWS Glue Data Catalog; configuring the crawler to 'Crawl new sub-folders only' or triggering it via S3 Event Notifications dramatically reduces crawl runtime and cost. Why Distractors Fail: Option B (AWS Glue Schema Registry, with one registered schema per dataset....) fails to satisfy the specific performance, security, or managed-service constraint stated in the prompt. Option C (An Apache Hive metastore on Amazon RDS shared by all three engines....) fails to satisfy the specific performance, security, or managed-service constraint stated in the prompt. Option D (Amazon SageMaker Catalog, with each dataset published as an asset....) fails to satisfy the specific performance, security, or managed-service constraint stated in the prompt.
questions.use_case: Data lake teams configure Glue Crawlers with a RecrawlPolicy of CRAWL_NEW_FOLDERS_ONLY (or CRAWL_EVENT_MODE via SQS/S3 events) to register new daily partitions in seconds.
questions.hack: Speed up slow Glue Crawlers on massive S3 buckets = Crawl new sub-folders only OR use S3 Event Notifications + SQS event-driven crawlers.

questions.stem: [A retail banking fraud-analytics group migrating legacy data warehouse workloads to AWS has a data engineer who] A healthcare company stores medical imaging files in Amazon S3. Each file is accessed roughly once per quarter, but when a physician requests an image it must be returned with millisecond latency. The enterprise wants the lowest-cost storage class that meets this requirement. Which storage class should a data engineer choose?
options: S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
S3 Standard-IA.
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
questions.explanation: - **a** Deep Archive is the cheapest class but standard retrievals take up to 12 hours, which fails the millisecond-latency requirement. - **b** Standard-IA also provides millisecond access, but its storage price is higher than Glacier Instant Retrieval, so it is not the lowest-cost option for data touched only quarterly. - **c** Glacier Instant Retrieval offers the lowest storage cost among classes that still return objects in milliseconds, and it is designed for data accessed roughly once per quarter. - **d** Glacier Flexible Retrieval requires an asynchronous restore that takes minutes to hours, so it cannot serve images with millisecond latency. **The concept.** S3 offers a spectrum of storage classes that trade storage price against retrieval latency and retrieval cost. The archive classes split into Glacier Instant Retrieval (milliseconds), Glacier Flexible Retrieval (minutes to hours), and Glacier Deep Archive (hours). **Why this is correct.** The access pattern is rare (quarterly) but latency-sensitive (milliseconds). Glacier Instant Retrieval was built exactly for this: archive-level storage pricing with the same millisecond first-byte latency as Standard-IA. Standard-IA meets the latency bar but costs more to store, while Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive are asynchronous-restore classes that can never satisfy an interactive request. **How to reason it out** 1. List the hard requirement: millisecond retrieval eliminates any class that needs an asynchronous restore (Flexible Retrieval, Deep Archive). 2. Compare the remaining synchronous classes (Standard, Standard-IA, One Zone-IA, Glacier Instant Retrieval) on storage price for rarely accessed data. 3. Choose Glacier Instant Retrieval because it has the lowest storage cost of the synchronous classes and targets data accessed about once a quarter. > **Exam tip:** When data is rarely accessed but must stay instantly retrievable, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval is the lowest-cost fit. Architectural Deep Dive: AWS STS (Security Token Service) issues short-lived temporary credentials (`AccessKeyId`, `SecretAccessKey`, `SessionToken`) via `AssumeRole` (cross-account or IAM role switching, using `ExternalId` in the trust policy when granting third-party SaaS vendors access to prevent the Confused Deputy problem), `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` (OIDC/mobile federation via Cognito), and `AssumeRoleWithSaml`. Why Distractors Fail: Option A (S3 Glacier Deep Archive....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and routes multi-gigabyte file uploads through a Lambda function or EC2 web tier instead of generating an S3 Pre-Signed URL for direct client-to-S3 upload, or forgets that S3 Pre-Signed URLs inherit the exact IAM permissions and session expiration of the principal that generated them. Option B (S3 Standard-IA....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and routes multi-gigabyte file uploads through a Lambda function or EC2 web tier instead of generating an S3 Pre-Signed URL for direct client-to-S3 upload, or forgets that S3 Pre-Signed URLs inherit the exact IAM permissions and session expiration of the principal that generated them. Option D (S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and routes multi-gigabyte file uploads through a Lambda function or EC2 web tier instead of generating an S3 Pre-Signed URL for direct client-to-S3 upload, or forgets that S3 Pre-Signed URLs inherit the exact IAM permissions and session expiration of the principal that generated them.
questions.use_case: When granting a third-party monitoring SaaS platform read-only access to your AWS account, you create an IAM Role in your account trusting the vendor's AWS account ID with a `sts:ExternalId` condition matching the unique ID provided by the vendor.
questions.hack: Third-party cross-account access + prevent Confused Deputy = IAM Role + `sts:AssumeRole` + `sts:ExternalId` condition.

questions.stem: [an AdTech real-time bidding platform processing high-velocity impression logs in AWS] An Amazon Redshift warehouse has a 2 GB product dimension that is updated weekly. Five large fact tables join to it on product_id, but each fact table is distributed on a different column (customer_id, order_id and others). Query plans show the dimension being broadcast across the network for every join. How should a data engineer change the product dimension?
options: Define a compound sort key on the dimension's product_id.
Set DISTSTYLE EVEN on the product dimension table.
Set DISTSTYLE ALL on the product dimension table.
Set DISTSTYLE KEY on the dimension's product_id column.
questions.explanation: - **a** A sort key orders rows within each slice for block pruning; it does not change which node holds a row, so the broadcast remains. - **b** EVEN spreads the dimension round-robin with no regard to the join column, so every join still has to broadcast or redistribute it. - **c** Correct. A full copy of a small, rarely updated dimension sits on every node, so each fact table finds every product row locally whatever the fact table is distributed on. - **d** KEY collocates only with tables distributed on the same column. The fact tables are distributed on other columns, so their matching rows are still on different slices. **The concept.** Redshift distribution decides which node stores each row. KEY collocates rows with the same value of one column, ALL puts a full copy on every node, EVEN round-robins, and AUTO lets Redshift choose. **Why this is correct.** The dimension is small and changes weekly, and it is joined from several fact tables that are each distributed on a different column. KEY on product_id would collocate with none of them, because a fact table distributed on customer_id keeps its product rows spread across all slices. ALL makes a local copy available on every node, so the broadcast step disappears for every fact table at the cost of a few GB per node and slower weekly loads. EVEN does nothing for joins, and a sort key only orders rows inside a slice. **How to reason it out** 1. Note the table's size and update rate: small and rarely changed. 2. Check what the fact tables are distributed on: different columns, none of them product_id. 3. Rule out KEY on the dimension, since collocation needs both sides distributed on the join column. 4. Choose ALL so every node holds the dimension and no join needs to move it. > **Exam tip:** Small, slowly changing dimensions joined from facts with different distribution keys get DISTSTYLE ALL. Architectural Deep Dive: Amazon Redshift optimizes analytical MPP queries using Distribution Styles (KEY for large joined tables on the join column, ALL for small dimension tables, EVEN for tables without clear join keys, or AUTO), Sort Keys (Compound for prefix-ordered filters vs Interleaved for equal-weight multi-column filters), Redshift Spectrum for querying exabytes in S3 without loading, and Concurrency Scaling for burst read traffic. Why Distractors Fail: Option A (Define a compound sort key on the dimension's product_id....) fails to satisfy the specific performance, security, or managed-service constraint stated in the prompt. Option B (Set DISTSTYLE EVEN on the product dimension table....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and chooses an anti-pattern distribution style (such as ALL on a multi-billion-row fact table) or loads cold archival data onto expensive cluster storage instead of querying via Redshift Spectrum. Option D (Set DISTSTYLE KEY on the dimension's product_id column....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and chooses an anti-pattern distribution style (such as ALL on a multi-billion-row fact table) or loads cold archival data onto expensive cluster storage instead of querying via Redshift Spectrum.
questions.use_case: Enterprise BI warehouses use COPY from S3 with manifest files for bulk loads, KEY distribution on shared high-cardinality join keys to eliminate DS_BCAST_INNER / DS_DIST_BOTH network redistribution, and WLM Query Monitoring Rules (QMR) to abort runaway queries.
questions.hack: Redshift Golden Rules: Large joined fact tables = KEY dist on join col; small dimension = ALL; burst BI users = Concurrency Scaling; query S3 directly without loading = Redshift Spectrum.

questions.stem: [A telecommunications carrier analyzing network tower CDR (call detail record) streams on AWS has a data engineer who] A nightly pipeline is driven by one AWS Lambda function that starts an AWS Glue job, polls GetJobRun in a sleep loop until the job ends, and then starts the next job. As data grew, one job now runs about 50 minutes and the function times out. The team wants per-step retries, a failure branch, one inspectable record of each run, and nothing billed while the pipeline is idle. What should the data platform engineer do?
options: Implement the workflow using a provisioned Amazon MWAA environment with a DAG that runs each Glue job.
Implement the workflow using a EventBridge rule on Glue Job State Change events to invoke the next step.
Have the function re-invoke itself asynchronously with the job run ID to keep polling.
Implement the workflow using a Step Functions Standard workflow that runs each Glue job with the .sync pattern.
questions.explanation: - **a** Airflow would give retries, failure handling and a run view, but a provisioned MWAA environment is billed per environment-hour for as long as it exists, including the hours between nightly runs, which breaks the nothing-billed-while-idle requirement. (Amazon MWAA Serverless removes that idle charge, but it is not what this option proposes.) - **b** Event-driven chaining removes the polling and costs nothing while idle, but each step becomes an independent invocation. Nothing ties the steps into one run with a shared history, and retries and failure routing across steps would have to be hand-built. - **c** Self-reinvocation gets past the 15-minute limit, but it is still hand-rolled orchestration: no declarative retries, no failure branch, no single record of the run, and every hop pays for compute that only waits. - **d** Correct. The run-a-job (.sync) integration makes the state wait for the Glue job to finish without any paid compute polling, each state takes its own Retry and Catch, every execution keeps a full event history, and Standard workflows bill per state transition with nothing running between executions. **The concept.** Orchestrating a multi-step pipeline means waiting for long-running jobs, retrying and routing failures, and keeping a record of each run. The orchestrator that does all of that without paying for idle time is serverless Step Functions with the run-a-job integration. **Why this is correct.** Two of the options remove the timeout, but the constraints decide. EventBridge chaining is serverless and idle-free, yet it has no notion of a run, so there is no single inspectable record and no declarative failure branch across steps. A provisioned MWAA environment provides all the orchestration features but bills per environment-hour, including while idle. A self-reinvoking Lambda only moves the polling problem around. A Step Functions Standard workflow with the Glue startJobRun.sync integration waits natively for the job, attaches Retry and Catch to each state, records every execution's history, and charges per state transition, so it is the only option that meets every requirement. **How to reason it out** 1. List the requirements: wait for long jobs, per-step retries, a failure branch, one record per run, no idle cost. 2. Rule out options that are still hand-written orchestration (polling or self-reinvoking Lambda). 3. Check the event-driven chain against 'one record per run' and the provisioned Airflow environment against 'nothing billed while idle'. 4. Choose the serverless orchestrator whose .sync integration waits for the job without paid polling. > **Exam tip:** When a Lambda function is polling a long job, the fix is Step Functions with the .sync integration, not a longer or self-chaining function. Architectural Deep Dive: Amazon MWAA (Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow) runs open-source Apache Airflow DAGs written in Python for complex cross-platform data orchestration, whereas AWS Step Functions provides serverless visual state-machine orchestration (Standard Workflows for long-running up to 1 year and Express Workflows for high-volume <5 minute event processing). Why Distractors Fail: Option A (Implement the workflow using a provisioned Amazon MWAA environment with a D...) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and uses a non-replayable delivery buffer or competing queue where multiple independent consumers cannot replay historical stream records at their own pace. Option B (Implement the workflow using a EventBridge rule on Glue Job State Change ev...) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and provisions unmanaged EC2 cron servers that lack dependency retries, dead-letter handling, and visual execution state tracking. Option C (Have the function re-invoke itself asynchronously with the job run ID to ke...) fails to satisfy the specific performance, security, or managed-service constraint stated in the prompt.
questions.use_case: Teams migrating existing Python Airflow DAGs to AWS choose Amazon MWAA; teams building new AWS-native serverless ETL pipelines with native Glue/Athena/EMR/Lambda SDK integrations and Distributed Map (up to 10,000 parallel executions) choose AWS Step Functions.
questions.hack: Existing Apache Airflow Python DAGs / cross-cloud portability = Amazon MWAA. Serverless AWS-native orchestration / Distributed Map over S3 = AWS Step Functions.

questions.stem: [a pharmaceutical clinical-trial data platform enforcing strict HIPAA governance on AWS] A data engineering team is migrating an on-premises Apache Airflow deployment to AWS. The team has more than 200 existing Python DAGs that use custom Airflow operators and plugins, and the team wants to keep the DAG code largely unchanged while AWS manages the underlying scheduler and worker infrastructure. Which service should the team use?
options: Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA)
Amazon EventBridge Scheduler.
AWS Glue workflows.
AWS Step Functions.
questions.explanation: - **a** Correct. MWAA runs open-source Apache Airflow as a managed service, so existing DAGs, custom operators, and plugins can be reused with minimal changes while AWS manages the scheduler, workers, and web server. - **b** EventBridge Scheduler invokes individual targets on a schedule. It has no concept of multi-step dependencies, DAGs, or Airflow compatibility. - **c** Glue workflows orchestrate only Glue jobs, crawlers, and triggers. They cannot run arbitrary Airflow DAGs or custom Python operators. - **d** Step Functions defines workflows in Amazon States Language (JSON), not Python DAGs, so all 200 workflows would have to be rewritten from scratch. **The concept.** Amazon MWAA is managed open-source Apache Airflow, which makes it the natural landing zone for teams that already have an Airflow investment they want to preserve. **Why this is correct.** The deciding constraint is the existing asset: 200 Python DAGs with custom operators and plugins. MWAA runs genuine Apache Airflow, so the team uploads DAGs to an S3 bucket, declares dependencies in requirements.txt, ships plugins in plugins.zip, and the code runs essentially unchanged while AWS operates the scheduler, workers, metadata database, and web server. Step Functions would force a full rewrite into Amazon States Language, Glue workflows only chain Glue-native components, and EventBridge Scheduler is a trigger mechanism rather than an orchestrator. **How to reason it out** 1. Identify the existing investment: Python DAGs, custom operators, and plugins that the team wants to keep. 2. Map that requirement to MWAA, the only AWS service that runs real Apache Airflow code. 3. Eliminate Step Functions (different workflow language), Glue workflows (Glue-only scope), and EventBridge Scheduler (triggering, not orchestration). > **Exam tip:** When a scenario mentions existing Airflow DAGs that must be preserved, the answer is Amazon MWAA. Why Distractors Fail: Option B (Amazon EventBridge Scheduler....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and provisions unmanaged EC2 cron servers that lack dependency retries, dead-letter handling, and visual execution state tracking. Option C (AWS Glue workflows....) fails to satisfy the specific performance, security, or managed-service constraint stated in the prompt. Option D (AWS Step Functions....) is incorrect because that service applies to a different workload pattern and provisions unmanaged EC2 cron servers that lack dependency retries, dead-letter handling, and visual execution state tracking.
